extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent office staff handling deposits of biological material for patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural requirements for depositing biological material (microorganisms, cell lines, etc.) in connection with patent applications, including timing, required disclosures, storage duration, and conditions for furnishing samples across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to deposit when invention involves non-public biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit of biological material must be made if an invention which involves the use of or concerns biological material is not disclosed in a manner which is clear enough and complete for the invention to be performed by a person skilled in the art, or where the material is not generally available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in multiple national provisions (e.g., GB Patents Rules 2007; Sweden Patents Act, Section 8a; EPO Rule 31(1)(a); Switzerland LBI Article 50a). Where the invention cannot be sufficiently described, deposit supplements the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit with an authorized/recognized depositary institution (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample of the biological material must be deposited with a depositary institution recognized as such under the Budapest Treaty (or with an institution recognized by the national patent office to meet the same requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jurisdictions require deposit 'with a recognized depositary institution' (Switzerland, Sweden, Spain, US, EPO). National patent offices often publish a list of acceptable institutions (EPO, Sweden, UK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of deposit — general rule (no later than filing date / priority date)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit must be made not later than the filing date of the patent application (or, where priority is claimed, by the priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stated for Spain, Sweden, EPO, Ukraine, MK (Macedonia) and others. Some jurisdictions allow narrow additional time for filing evidence in limited circumstances (e.g., Macedonia: evidence may be filed additionally for valid reasons within 90 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: United States time of deposit (USPTO exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO rules the deposit must be made by the time the patent issue fee is paid, but the USPTO strongly encourages deposit on or before the filing date of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR provisions cited (1.804, 1.809(c)); Manual of Patent Examining Procedure guidance distinguishes the statutory deadline from best practice (encouraged earlier deposit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must state deposit details (institution, date, accession number)
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the depositary institution, the date where the material was deposited and the accession number of the deposit should be given in the specification of the patent application or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GB Patents Rules 2007; Switzerland OBI Article 45b; EPO requires depositary institution and accession number (Rule 31 EPC). The latest date to add such information is subject to specific time limits (see related criterion on time-limits for submission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must include essential characteristics / reference to deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention entails the manufacture or use of biological material and cannot be sufficiently described, the disclosure shall be supplemented by the deposit of a sample and in the description by information relating to the essential characteristics of that material and by a reference to the deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit in Swiss law (LBI Article 50a) and reflected in other statutes requiring available descriptive information in addition to deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: If depositor is different, submit evidence of authorization and unreserved consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the biological material has been deposited by a person other than the applicant, the application must state the name and address of the depositor and a document must be submitted providing evidence that the depositor has authorized the applicant to refer to the deposited biological material and has given his unreserved and irrevocable consent to the deposited material being made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO Rule 31(1)(c),(d) EPC; this ensures the EPO can publish and make samples available even when deposit was made by a third party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-limits for adding deposit information to the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit information may be submitted within specified time limits (commonly within 16 months after filing or priority date, or before technical preparations for publication are complete), with jurisdictional variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO: within 16 months after filing/priority or before technical preparations for publication (Rule 31(2) EPC). GB: latest date whatever first expires of 16 months after priority/filing, or applicant's request for accelerated publication, or one month after comptroller notification under section 118(4). Submission is considered to constitute unreserved and irrevocable consent where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage governed by Budapest Treaty (minimum 30 years / related minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of storage is governed by Rule 9 of the Regulations under the Budapest Treaty; the duration of storage shall be a minimum of 30 years (and certain national rules also require at least five years after the most recent request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switzerland, US, Ukraine and others explicitly apply Rule 9 and a 30-year minimum; some national entries record 'no provision' where domestic law is silent and Treaty rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of samples — at grant / publication / when application made available
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing for making samples available varies: samples become available on grant of the patent (US); as from the date on which the patent application is made available to the public (Sweden); after publication by any person (UK) — with pre-publication access often limited to entitled persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See country-specific rules: US (37 CFR 1.808) ties availability to grant (with possible earlier access if USPTO determines entitlement); Sweden and EPO refer to availability when application is made available to the public (commonly after 18 months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication access restricted to persons entitled to inspect files / specified categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publication, access to deposited biological material may be limited to persons entitled to inspect the files under applicable law (e.g., Article 44 in Spain) or to persons who have made the required requests and meet statutory entitlement criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spain: before first publication only to persons having the right to inspect files; UK: before publication, only persons to whom section 118(4) applies and who have made a request; such pre-publication access routes and criteria differ by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requester's undertaking: non-disclosure and experimental-use limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to samples is provided only if the requester undertakes during the time the patent application is valid not to make the biological material or derived material available to any third party and to use that material for experimental purposes only (unless the applicant/proprietor expressly waives such undertaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undertaking requirement is widely used (Spain Article 45; Switzerland Article 45g; UK Patents Rules Schedule 1 paragraph 5). Some jurisdictions provide exceptions (e.g., not required where material is used under a compulsory license in Switzerland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-only access at applicant's request; expert list and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee/applicant may request that a sample be available only to an expert until the application is laid open to public inspection or finally decided; experts are typically selected from a patent-office-published list or may be nominated, and must give required undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK: notice on Form 8A to limit access to an expert; Sweden: experts listed by the patent office; Spain: issue of a sample to an expert nominated by the applicant; experts must submit written statements/undertakings and the applicant may object to a particular expert within a time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of expert-only restriction and post-withdrawal access to experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions limiting issuance of samples to experts may last until grant or, in case of withdrawal or refusal, access may be limited to an independent expert for a period (commonly 20 years from filing) upon request of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spain Article 45(3) and Sweden/UK provisions: expert-only restrictions can persist for 20 years from filing if application is withdrawn or refused; applicants may secure long-term expert-only access by following formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement deposit procedure where material ceases to be viable
rubrics_metrics.description: If a deposited biological material ceases to be viable or a sample cannot be supplied, it may be replaced by a new deposit of the same biological material within the time and manner prescribed; the new deposit is considered to have been made when the earlier deposit was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sweden explicitly allows replacement with retroactive dating (Patents Act Section 8a). UK requires a new deposit within three months of notification/advertisement if material ceases to be available, accompanied by signed statement that it is the same material and amendment of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of unavailability — insufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the material is no longer available at the depositary authority and is not transferred or re-deposited within required timeframes, the invention may be considered not to be described in a sufficiently precise and complete way and the application could be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macedonia's provision: unavailability without timely re-deposit can lead to the invention not being sufficiently disclosed; other offices require timely corrective action to avoid such consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for requesting samples (forms, statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for samples must follow prescribed forms and include required statements/undertakings (e.g., UK Patents Form 8; Sweden requires written request plus prescribed statement to prevent misuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance (correct forms, contents, and timelines) is necessary for obtaining samples; applicant/proprietor has limited time to object to expert nominations after a request is sent to the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office determination/certification of entitlement to samples during pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: During pendency, a deposited biological material may be made available if the patent office determines the person requesting a sample to be entitled; the office then issues the certification required by the Budapest Treaty and notifies the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US (37 CFR 1.808(a)(1)): USPTO will determine entitlement, make the Rule 11.3(a) certification and send copies of the request and certification to the filer. This is a gatekeeping function to enable pre-grant access in exceptional/entitled cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrevocable removal of public-access restrictions upon grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Any restriction of public access to samples of deposited biological material must be irrevocably removed as of the date of grant of the relevant patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US rule (37 CFR 1.808(a)(2)) states restrictions are removed at grant. Other jurisdictions similarly provide that applicant's ability to restrict public access ends on grant (though some had specific 20-year transitional provisions for withdrawn applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/listing of recognized depositary institutions and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent offices publish lists of institutions recognized as depositary authorities and lists of experts who may receive expert-only samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO publishes a list in its Official Journal (Rule 33(6) EPC); Sweden and the UK also maintain lists and procedures for listing/appointing experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special national procedural flexibilities (e.g., evidence filing windows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions allow limited additional time or specific remedial filings where deposit evidence or re-deposit is required — for example, Macedonia allows filing evidence for valid reasons within 90 days, or re-deposit windows where depositary authority loses status (with specified notification/advertisement triggers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions create narrowly-defined procedural reliefs; applicants must follow the precise national timelines and notification protocols to preserve rights.
